answer: An index assembled from document revisions that never coexisted has no single point-in-time source state behind it. Each retrieved section, score and citation can be individually real, yet the joint evidence set was never simultaneously valid: older and newer wording can be blended into an internally plausible composite, stale and current claims can appear side by side, and provenance fields such as source revision, access date and access labels cannot be anchored to one snapshot. Because results still resolve to real canonical documents and rank plausibly, per-citation verification can pass while the combined answer asserts a corpus state that never existed; the reader cannot tell which revision was authoritative for the question, and re-running against any valid snapshot will not reproduce the answer. Mixed access labels compound the problem when permissions changed between revisions. The book's contract makes index generations belong to an admitted source revision and access scope: define rebuild consistency for source changes mid-build, validate a candidate generation before promotion, pin queries to one generation, resolve every result back to canonical source evidence, and retire old generations safely. Provenance must distinguish cited from actually read sources, record revision or access date against the question's version requirement, and separate direct evidence, inference and missing or contradictory sources.
